newsitem.title: THAILAND: Crunch comes closer for Thai finance firms.
newsitem.headline: Crunch comes closer for Thai finance firms.

text.p: Thailand's finance sector may have muddled through last week's crisis of confidence, but it still faces a long and painful cure that could see many firms swallowed up or backed to the wall, analysts said on Monday.
"People have been talking about an overhaul of finance firms for the past five years," said one analyst at a Thai securities and finance house.
"This crisis has simply brought the crunch-time closer," he said, adding that improvements to the country's financial system had failed to keep pace with its stellar economic growth.
Authorities stepped in last week to halt a surge of deposit withdrawals from the finance companies, whose liquidity and bad debt problems suddenly came under the spotlight.
But the government, already on a budget blitz, has made it clear that free bailouts are not on offer.
It says the next steps to better health will have to be taken by the institutions themselves and, warning of growing competition from abroad, is recommending a rash of mergers.

The 91 finance firms, about half of which are fiercely independent family businesses, have long resisted calls for rationalisation of their industry. Few saw the need for change when profits were riding high on the back of an economic boom.

"Because it's been so profitable, they haven't felt the need or urge to merge," said Surakiat Wongwasin, president of Multi-Credit Corporation of Thailand. "They haven't reached that level of pain yet."

Finance firms are also wary about teaming up with each other because of the difficulties of agreeing on asset prices. When two firms merge, one would have to give up its most valuable asset -- its licence to operate.
Another obstacle was the swingeing tax that would hit shareholders in the case of a merger, said Dhana Siam Finance and Securities Co president Rutt Phanijphand.

Last week's announcement of a friendly merger between Finance One Plc and Thai Danu Bank Plc focused attention on the troubles of a sector which has sunk 25 percent of its lending into the slumping property market.
FinOne is the country's biggest finance company and was previously thought to be in good shape

One foreign analyst estimated that at least 8.8 percent of bank and finance company loans were classified as doubtful or sub-standard assets and that their low quality would deteriorate further as the real estate crisis dragged on.
Now, under new regulations, the finance firms will be required to detail non-performing loans in their balance sheets from mid-1997.
The implicit message is -- if the companies don't shape up soon, investors may see to it that they go down.
Surakiat said the industry should shoot for half the number of players within two years, but said it would be even better if there were just 20 firms in business by then.
The authorities say their push for rationalisation comes with carrots as well as sticks.
Many hope expect the carrot to be a more level playing field in the finance industry as a whole, with those strong enough to survive winning licences to compete in more conventional areas of banking.
